title: A crown you tie yourself
told: a sakhi from Guru Gobind Singh’s childhood

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? do you wear anything that tells people who you are?
options: then you know the questions people ask. listen.
then you know the feeling. listen.
then this one might surprise you. listen.

steps.line: Long ago in Patna, by the river Ganges, a little boy played on the riverbank. He would grow up to be the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: One day he slipped off his gold bangle and tossed it into the river.
His mother hurried down to the water. Where did it fall? Show me.

steps.q: The boy wants to show her where it fell. How do you think he does it?
o: Throws the other bangle in too
Wades in to look for it
steps.why: He threw the second one in. Right there.

steps.line: So he tossed in the other one too. Right there, he said.

steps.q: Why do you think Sikhs still tell this little story?
o: To show gold didn’t hold him, even young
To show how spoiled rich children were
To explain why Sikhs avoid gold
steps.why: Gold didn’t hold him, even as a boy. The spot is still remembered at Gurdwara Kangan Ghat in Patna, kangan meaning bangle.

steps.q: He grew up to be the tenth Guru, and in 1699 founded the Khalsa. Khalsa once meant land held straight from the king, with no lord between. Why that word?
o: Sikhs answer to God, with no one between
He meant to claim land from the emperor
It marked them as his royal guard
steps.why: Khalsa comes from a Persian word for crown land. A Sikh of the Khalsa belongs to God and Guru directly: no middleman, no caste, no lord.

steps.line: In his day, fine turbans marked kings and nobles. The Guru asked every Sikh to keep their hair and cover it. A crown for every family.
Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut, called kesh, and tie a turban, the dastaar, fresh each morning. On the wrist, a kara: plain steel.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Many Sikhs wear the kara on the hand they use most. What is it there to remind them?
o: That they come from a warrior family
That their hands should do only good
That steel is stronger than gold
steps.why: It catches the eye just before that hand acts. A circle with no end, like the One God.

steps.q: Tradition says the Guru gave every Sikh man the name Singh, lion. What name did he give every woman?
steps.why: Kaur is often translated princess. Every Sikh shares a royal name, so no surname can mark their caste.

say: here’s what i love. a boy who tossed his gold into a river grew up to hand every sikh a crown.
that’s the turban: not a hat, not wealth. a crown you tie yourself. and if you’ve cut your hair, you’re every bit as welcome here.

steps.q: A boy who threw his gold away later gave every Sikh a crown. So what kind of crown is the turban?
o: A sign of a family’s wealth
A reward for the most devout
steps.why: Not gold, not rank. A crown you tie yourself, open to every family.

today.say: many sikhs say the kara reminds the hand to do only good. today, before one choice, touch your wrist and ask: is this good?
options: one touch, one question. that’s the kara.
then today, let it ask out loud.
